ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Lake Charles, LA for refinery, chemical and LNG piping, vessels and tanks. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Lake Charles, Louisiana
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Lake Charles for ultrasonic thickness testing of piping, vessels and storage tanks, and for angle-beam ultrasonic weld inspection on pressure and structural steel. The work is built around the Calcasieu Ship Channel industrial corridor: refineries, chemical complexes, LNG facilities and the marine terminals that serve them. Send the component list, the code and the access plan, and request a UT inspection quote for Lake Charles.

Why ultrasonic testing matters in the Lake Charles corridor

Southwest Louisiana is one of the densest industrial areas in the country. The Calcasieu Ship Channel runs about 68 miles from Lake Charles to the Gulf of Mexico, at roughly 40 feet deep and 400 feet wide, and along it sit petroleum refineries, chemical manufacturing plants, natural gas installations, pipelines and LNG export facilities. Marine terminals handle petrochemical, bulk and project cargo. Plants here run continuously for years between major outages, and almost everything inside them is a steel pressure boundary that slowly loses wall to corrosion and erosion.

That makes thickness monitoring the heartbeat of Lake Charles integrity work. Crude and product piping, heater and boiler tubes, overhead lines on pipe racks, reactor and column shells, storage tank shells and floors, and cooling-water systems are all measured at regular intervals and compared against a minimum required thickness. Ultrasonic testing is the standard way to take those readings while the equipment is in service, and it is the standard volumetric method for checking new and repaired welds where the code and the owner permit it.

Damage mechanisms ultrasonic work looks for

The Gulf Coast environment adds its own pressures. Warm, humid, salt-laden air drives external corrosion on carbon steel. Insulated lines are prone to corrosion under insulation, where water gets under the jacket and attacks the pipe unseen. Inside the pipe, the process decides the damage: sulfur-bearing crude drives wall loss in refinery piping, acid and caustic services attack vessel shells and nozzles, and flow-accelerated erosion thins elbows, reducers and tees downstream of valves. Cooling-water systems pit and scale.

A thickness survey tells the owner how much wall is left at each monitoring location and how fast it is going. A careful technician also looks for localized attack: grid readings around an elbow, a ring of readings on a dead leg, or a scan across a suspected thinning band rather than a single point. The aim is to find the thinnest spot, not to confirm the nominal pipe wall. Ultrasonic testing cannot reveal the cause of the thinning, so the owner's integrity team uses the data together with process knowledge.

Codes and regulations that govern the work

Process piping in the corridor is usually built and examined under ASME B31.3, and power piping under B31.1. Pressure vessels follow ASME Section VIII, with Division 1 Appendix 12 covering ultrasonic examination of welds. Method requirements sit in ASME Section V: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials, and Article 23 for the contact thickness standard SE-797. ASTM E797 and ASTM E164 give the practices for thickness and for contact examination of weldments. In-service equipment is inspected under the owner's program based on API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for aboveground storage tanks. In every case the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection conclusion, and our role is to produce the thickness and indication data that inspector relies on.

At the state level, Louisiana's boiler rules are administered by the Boiler Inspection Section of the Office of State Fire Marshal. The state adopts the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code as its construction code, and inspectors there and at insurers carry National Board commissions. Units that fall under those rules are inspected by a commissioned inspector, and our readings support that person's inspection. Federal process safety rules under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) also require owners to keep an inspection and testing program based on good engineering practice, which is where regular thickness surveys fit.

How thickness testing is done in refineries and chemical plants

The technician starts from the owner's condition monitoring locations, or CMLs, on isometric drawings or equipment sketches. Each CML is marked on the pipe so the same spot can be read year after year. Readings are taken with a dual-element probe, which is better than a single-crystal probe on rough or corroded surfaces because its separated crystals reduce noise near the surface. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same alloy before the job, checked again at the end of the day, and the A-scan is watched on pitted surfaces to avoid locking onto a false echo.

Surface condition and temperature need attention on hot lines. Where a surface is above the range of standard probes, a high-temperature probe and suitable couplant are used, with temperature correction applied to the velocity. Insulation has to be removed at the CML or an inspection window opened by the owner's crew, and the cladding replaced afterward, so access, scaffolding and insulation work are planned with the survey. Our report gives the minimum reading at each location, plus the grid when the owner asks for one, and the owner's inspector calculates corrosion rate and remaining life.

Weld examination with angle beams

For groove welds, the technician uses shear-wave angle-beam probes, typically at 45, 60 or 70 degrees, set up on a calibration block with side-drilled holes to create a reference level or a distance-amplitude curve. The technician scans beside the weld to cover the weld volume and heat-affected zone and evaluates each indication for amplitude, length and position in the thickness. Acceptance follows the construction code, such as Section VIII Appendix 12 for vessels or the B31.3 criteria for piping.

Ultrasonic weld examination is used in the corridor on thick-wall piping butt welds, vessel shell and head seams, nozzle attachment welds and structural steel groove welds in pipe-rack and equipment-module construction. Substituting ultrasonics for another volumetric method on a code-required examination is an owner and engineer decision, agreed with the authorized inspector before work begins. We do not make that decision for a project, but we will help your team think it through and document it.

Tank farms and storage assets

Storage is a large part of the corridor's footprint. Product and crude tanks, spheres and bullets sit at refineries and terminals, and aboveground storage tank work is organized around API 653 inspections. For tank shells, ultrasonic thickness readings are taken in vertical strips from the bottom course to the top and compared with the minimum thickness the owner's inspector calculates for each course. Roof plates, annular rings and nozzle necks are also gauged. Floor corrosion is usually screened by other means, but ultrasonics confirms and sizes the thinnest spots once they are located. Operators schedule these surveys around tank cleaning and out-of-service periods, so we coordinate scaffolding or rope-free access with your team and keep the gauge locations marked for repeat surveys.

Spheres and pressurized storage add weld-seam work. Ultrasonic weld examination of selected seams can be requested by the owner as part of an in-service evaluation, using angle beams and the calibration blocks the procedure specifies.

Piping circuits and injection points

Within a unit, the high-risk piping circuits are known to the integrity team: injection points, mixing tees, dead legs, low points where water collects, and the outside radius of elbows after control valves. Ultrasonic surveys concentrate on those spots. Because corrosion at an injection point is often a narrow band, technicians scan the full circumference and a length of pipe either side rather than reading one point. On small-bore connections, where a conventional thickness probe is awkward, the technician selects a small-diameter probe and records the limits of what could be measured. These details of the survey are what make the data useful for a remaining life calculation.

Qualified people, and a second set of eyes

Atlantis technicians perform ultrasonic examinations under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician operates the instrument and judges the signals, and an ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews the report format, so each job has a qualified reviewer behind it. The employer, not a course provider, certifies personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so a client with its own written practice should tell us up front what it requires. Our Level III consulting and written practice development services can review an existing procedure or help prepare one for a project.

What you receive

Each report states the component, its tag or isometric number and the thickness location, the procedure and revision, the code and edition, and the acceptance criteria. It lists the instrument, probe, block and couplant, the calibration checks, the surface temperature on hot lines, and the technician's name and level. Thickness data is presented by location, with nominal thickness and the owner's minimum required thickness where provided. For welds, each recordable indication has its position, length and amplitude with the accept or reject disposition, plus a sketch of the scan plan. The format is built so another inspector can repeat the measurement later and compare.

Planning work in Lake Charles

The big scheduling variables are weather and plant access. Summers are hot and very humid, and afternoon thunderstorms are common, so outdoor scanning often starts early and needs dry, clean surfaces. Hurricane season runs through the fall, and the 2020 storms showed how long a disruption can last; plants shut down ahead of a storm, and rebuilding work created a long wave of inspection demand afterward. We build float into schedules and keep a flexible mobilization plan.

Site access can take time. Plants require orientation and safety training, contractor safety program registration such as ISNetworld, drug screening and badging, and some dock and terminal areas call for a TWIC credential. Confined space entry, hot work and scaffold permits are issued by the owner. Atlantis has no office in Lake Charles, so technicians travel to your site and lodging is part of the plan; please give us the shutdown dates early. Quote requests receive a reply within one business day.

Choosing UT, MT or PT in Lake Charles

Ultrasonic testing answers questions about wall thickness and buried weld flaws. When the issue is a surface crack in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Lake Charles is usually quicker. When the metal is stainless, duplex, nickel alloy or aluminum, liquid penetrant testing in Lake Charles is the practical surface method. Many outage jobs combine them: thickness at the base metal, MT or PT on the final weld surface. For Louisiana-wide planning, see our inspection services page for Louisiana. For method background, read the ultrasonic testing overview and the thickness measurement requirements summary.

Training in-house technicians

Plants and contractors in the Calcasieu area who want to build their own ultrasonic capability can use our UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 programs, the ultrasonic simulator and the Lake Charles training page.

faq.q: Can you measure wall thickness on insulated piping in Lake Charles?
faq.a: Yes, but the insulation has to be opened at each monitoring location, usually by the owner’s crew, and the cladding closed afterward. We plan the access and scaffolding with you before mobilizing.

faq.q: Do you have an office or crew in Lake Charles?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Lake Charles. Qualified technicians travel to your plant, terminal or yard for the agreed scope, and travel and site orientation are built into the plan.

faq.q: What codes do you follow for ultrasonic inspection of refinery and chemical piping?
faq.a: We work to the code your specification names: ASME B31.3 for process piping, Section VIII for vessels, and ASME Section V for the method. In-service work follows the owner’s API 510, 570 or 653 program.

faq.q: Who decides if a pipe is still fit for service after thickness testing?
faq.a: The owner’s authorized inspector and integrity engineer decide. We supply measured thickness data and a report with the method and calibration details so they can calculate corrosion rate and remaining life.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be done on hot lines while they are running?
faq.a: Yes, within the limits of safe access and the equipment. High-temperature probes and couplant are used, the surface temperature is recorded, and the calibration is corrected for temperature.

faq.q: What affects the accuracy of UT readings on corroded steel?
faq.a: Surface roughness, scale, coating, temperature and the calibration block all matter. A dual-element probe, a clean grid location and watching the A-scan help avoid false readings on pitted metal.

faq.q: Can ultrasonics replace another volumetric method on a weld in Lake Charles?
faq.a: Only where the code and the owner both allow it. That decision is agreed with the owner, the engineer of record and the authorized inspector before the job, since the acceptance criteria differ.

faq.q: What should I send to start a UT quote for Lake Charles?
faq.a: Send the component list or isometrics, material and thickness range, temperature, insulation status, the code and edition, plant access requirements, shutdown dates and any scaffold or permit details.

faq.q: Can you train our Lake Charles technicians in ultrasonics?
faq.a: Yes. Our UT Level 1 and Level 2 courses prepare candidates under SNT-TC-1A, and your company then certifies them under its written practice once the required experience hours are logged.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) | Lake Charles, LA
mt.description: Magnetic particle testing in Lake Charles, LA for pipe rack welds, pressure vessel attachments, lifting gear and dock steel. Ask for an MT quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) in Lake Charles, Louisiana
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT brings Level II magnetic particle testing to Lake Charles refineries, chemical plants, LNG construction sites and marine terminals. The technique finds surface-breaking and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, which covers most of the structural and pressure steel on the Calcasieu Ship Channel. Describe the welds or components, and request a magnetic particle testing quote for Lake Charles.

Where MT is used along the Calcasieu corridor

Lake Charles sits in the middle of one of the country's major energy and chemical corridors. Refineries, chemical plants and LNG export facilities line the ship channel, and port terminals handle bulk cargo, project cargo and imported wind energy equipment. Big construction projects and long maintenance outages keep a large workforce welding carbon steel year-round. That steel is exposed to salt air, humidity and cyclic loads, so surface cracks starting at weld toes, attachments and repairs are a real concern.

Typical MT work includes pipe-rack and equipment-module structural welds, attachment welds on pressure vessel shells such as clips, saddles and lifting lugs, nozzle reinforcement pad welds, and tank shell and floor repairs. Heavy-lift work generates its own demand: padeyes, spreader bars, shackle points and crane components need documented proof they are crack-free before a module or vessel is hoisted. Dock and wharf steel, handling equipment and mooring hardware at marine terminals are examined for fatigue cracking. Whenever a drawing or an inspector calls for a surface examination of a ferromagnetic weld, MT is fast and sensitive.

What MT detects, and what it does not

Magnetic particle testing uses the leakage of a magnetic field around a surface break in ferromagnetic metal. Fine iron particles, applied dry or in a liquid bath, collect where the field leaks and outline the flaw. It detects cracks, laps, seams and some lack-of-fusion at or very near the surface, even when they are too tight to see. It is quick, shows results immediately and requires little surface preparation beyond cleaning.

It has firm limits. The material must be ferromagnetic, which means carbon steel, low-alloy steel and the martensitic and ferritic grades. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, duplex stainless, nickel alloys, aluminum or titanium, and many chemical plants in Lake Charles use such alloys, so those components go to liquid penetrant testing in Lake Charles. MT also cannot size depth or find deep subsurface flaws. Heavy coatings, thick scale and weld spatter weaken the indication or hide it, so surfaces are cleaned first.

Governing codes

ASME Section V Article 7 covers the MT method, ASTM E709 is the general guide and ASTM E1444 is the practice. Pressure vessel work to ASME Section VIII Division 1 uses Appendix 6 for MT methods and acceptance. Process piping under ASME B31.3 uses its examination section and the acceptance table 341.3.2. Structural steel and many pipe-rack welds follow AWS D1.1. For aboveground storage tanks, repair welds are examined under the owner's API 653 program with the authorized inspector responsible for the final decision. Our report supplies the examination record to support that decision.

Louisiana adds its own layer for boilers and pressure vessels. The Office of State Fire Marshal's Boiler Inspection Section administers the state's rules, which adopt the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code as the Louisiana construction code and rely on commissioned inspectors. A weld repair on a unit that comes under those rules is reported to the owner and the commissioned inspector. Our summary of Article 7 requirements sets out the method controls in detail.

Technique in practice

Field MT in Lake Charles is usually done with an AC electromagnetic yoke because it is portable, can be moved along a weld quickly and works on rough surfaces. ASME Section V requires that an AC yoke show at least ten pounds of lifting power at the maximum pole spacing, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least forty pounds, verified on a test weight before work starts. The technician examines each area twice, rotating the yoke about ninety degrees, so cracks in any direction cross the field. Between passes the particles are applied lightly, blown clear of excess and examined while the field is applied.

Dry powder is convenient outdoors in warm weather, though wind scatters it, and it is poorly suited to damp surfaces. Wet visible or fluorescent particles give higher sensitivity on smooth surfaces and on welds ground flush. Fluorescent work needs UV-A light and a darkened area, so a shaded tent or enclosure on a sunny pipe rack is normal. Prods are used on thick sections when yokes cannot reach, with care to avoid arc burns on finished surfaces. When residual magnetism could cause trouble in later welding or machinery, the part is demagnetized and tested with a field indicator.

Surface preparation and contamination

Gulf Coast steel arrives at the inspection with paint, rust, salt and sometimes grease. A technician removes loose scale and coating from the weld and about an inch on each side, or uses a procedure qualified for thin coatings. Wet particles need a clean, grease-free surface to flow properly, while dry powder needs a dry one. Humidity can dampen powder and cause it to clump on cold steel that has collected dew, so early-morning work often needs a wipe-down first.

Welds in the as-welded condition can have sharp toes and spatter that hold particles. A light grind agreed with the welding supervisor gives a cleaner reading, but grinding must not smear metal over a real crack, so the Level II decides what preparation is acceptable under the procedure.

Heavy-lift, module and project cargo work

The corridor's construction projects often involve modules, vessels and columns built elsewhere and brought in through the port, then lifted into place. Each lift depends on welded attachments: padeyes, trunnions, lifting lugs and tailing devices. The lift plan usually asks for those welds to be examined before the load is applied. MT on the lug weld, with the weld ground to a clean profile, gives the lift engineer a record that the weld was free of surface cracks. After the lift, temporary attachments are removed and the base metal ground smooth, and MT confirms that no gouges or cracks remain in the parent steel.

Imported project cargo, such as wind energy components and large fabricated assemblies, also arrives with shipping and handling attachments. When owners or insurers want the weld condition recorded after transit, a surface examination of the critical welds is a quick, low-disruption way to do it.

Marine terminals bring their own steel to the schedule. Dock structures, loading arms supports, crane rails and mooring fittings are exposed to salt spray and cyclic loading, and welded repairs on them are examined by MT where the steel is magnetic. A short written plan agreed before mobilization, listing weld locations, access method and the owner's acceptance code, avoids standby time once the technician is on the dock.

Records matter on these jobs as well. Each examined weld is tied to a map or a photograph so a later reviewer can find the same location, and indications that are repaired are re-examined and reported with the same identifier so the history stays together.

Pressure equipment attachments and repairs

On pressure equipment, external attachment welds are a common place for cracks to start, because they are located in areas of stress and heat input. Support clips, saddle welds, davit lugs, ladder and platform clips and insulation support rings all have welds that may be checked during an inspection or a repair. After a repair, the area is examined by MT again and the report notes the final disposition. Owners who run a mechanical integrity program under OSHA process safety rules use this record as evidence that repairs were verified. On carbon steel tank shells and nozzles, MT is also used on repair welds and on seams ground out for inspection, with the authorized inspector deciding on acceptance.

Because the method is fast, it suits outage conditions: a technician can examine a long run of weld in a short time, report indications immediately to the welding supervisor and let repairs proceed with little delay.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis MT technicians are qualified under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the equipment, performs the testing and interprets indications against the code. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report format. The employer is the certifying body under SNT-TC-1A, so the written practice of the technician's employer sets the limits of what they can sign. If you need a project-specific procedure or want an independent review of a contractor's MT, see our Level III consulting and written practice development.

The MT report

Reports identify the component by tag, drawing or weld number and note the procedure revision, code edition and acceptance standard. They record the magnetizing method, yoke or prod spacing, the lifting power verification, the particle type and carrier, the lighting for fluorescent work, and the technician's name and level. Each indication is logged with its location, orientation and length and marked accepted or rejected against the criteria. Sketches or photographs show the coverage, and demagnetization results are noted where required.

Planning MT jobs in Lake Charles

Weather drives much of the planning. Summer heat can make steel too hot for some particle suspensions, and high humidity and sudden thunderstorms interrupt outdoor work, so crews often start early and use shelters. Hurricane season brings plant shutdowns and lengthy recovery work, and the aftermath of the 2020 storms created a steady need for structural and repair weld checks. Because Atlantis has no office in the city, we mobilize technicians to your site and combine MT with other scopes when possible. Expect plant orientation, contractor safety registration, badging and, at some terminals, TWIC requirements. A quote request gets our reply within one business day.

MT, PT or UT for your Lake Charles job

Choose MT when the target is a surface crack in magnetic steel. Use liquid penetrant in Lake Charles for stainless, duplex and non-ferrous alloys, and ultrasonic testing in Lake Charles for wall thickness or buried weld flaws. Our MT versus PT comparison and the magnetic particle testing page give more detail, and the Louisiana inspection services page covers the wider state.

In-house MT training

Contractors and plants in the area can qualify their own staff through MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses and the Lake Charles training page, then certify them under the company's written practice.

faq.q: What parts of a refinery can MT be used on in Lake Charles?
faq.a: MT suits carbon and low-alloy steel welds and parts: pipe rack structure, vessel attachment welds, lifting lugs, nozzle pads and tank repair welds. It does not work on austenitic stainless or other non-magnetic alloys.

faq.q: Is wet or dry particle better for Gulf Coast conditions?
faq.a: Dry powder is handy on rough, warm, dry welds but wind and humidity hurt it. Wet particles give better sensitivity on cleaner surfaces. The procedure sets which is allowed, and we pick the one that suits the weld and the weather.

faq.q: Can you perform fluorescent MT outdoors in the heat?
faq.a: Fluorescent MT needs a darkened area and a UV-A light with the intensity the procedure specifies. We use a tent or enclosure in daylight, or switch to visible particles where the procedure and code allow it.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep inspectors in Lake Charles?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Lake Charles. We mobilize qualified technicians to your site, so please share the scope, dates and site access rules in your quote request.

faq.q: Which standard decides whether an MT indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The construction or repair code for your project decides, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, B31.3 for piping or AWS D1.1 for structural welds. Our report names the edition and criteria used.

faq.q: Why is each weld examined in two directions?
faq.a: A crack shows best when the magnetic field crosses it. Magnetizing in two directions about ninety degrees apart makes sure cracks running either way are caught.

faq.q: Do heavy lift components need MT before the pick?
faq.a: Many rigging plans and lift engineers ask for it on padeyes, lugs and spreaders. MT gives documented proof that the welds are free of surface cracks before the load is applied.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MT in Lake Charles?
faq.a: Send the list of welds or parts, material, coating, size range, code and edition, access and permit needs, shutdown dates and site safety requirements. A few photographs of the areas speed up planning.

faq.q: Can your courses prepare our welders and helpers for MT work?
faq.a: Our MT Level 1 and Level 2 courses are written for people entering NDT under SNT-TC-1A. Your company certifies employees under its written practice after the experience hours are completed.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Lake Charles, LA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection in Lake Charles, LA for stainless, duplex and nickel alloy welds, tubesheets and repairs. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Lake Charles, Louisiana
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing in Lake Charles for stainless steel, duplex, nickel alloy, titanium and aluminum welds, plus machined parts and repair surfaces. Many chemical, refining and LNG components in the Calcasieu corridor use corrosion-resistant alloys that magnetic particle methods cannot examine, which makes dye penetrant inspection a daily tool. Share the materials, the code and the access, and request a penetrant testing quote for Lake Charles.

Why penetrant testing is so common in Lake Charles plants

The industrial base around the Calcasieu Ship Channel is chemical-heavy. Along with petroleum refineries it includes plants making PVC and chlorine, polymers, titanium dioxide pigment, catalysts and glycols, and LNG facilities that liquefy natural gas at very low temperature for export. Those processes use aggressive chemistry and cryogenic service, and the piping, heat exchangers and vessels are often made from austenitic stainless steel, duplex stainless, nickel alloys, titanium or aluminum. None of those can be magnetized in the usual way, so PT is the standard check for surface cracks in their welds.

Examples of where it is used include weld overlays and clad surfaces in reactors and columns, stainless tubesheet welds in heat exchangers, cryogenic stainless piping at LNG facilities, alloy pump and valve repairs, and aluminum fittings and exchangers. On carbon steel, penetrant also helps where a magnetic method is awkward, such as small-bore connections, thin sections or threaded parts. During maintenance outages, penetrant is also a typical final check on ground-out defects and weld repairs of every material.

What penetrant testing reveals, and the cases where it fails

PT works by capillary action. A thin liquid is applied to the clean surface and enters any open crack, pit or lap. The excess is removed, then a developer draws the liquid back out to form a visible bleed-out. Visible red dye is examined in good white light, while fluorescent penetrant is examined under UV-A in a darkened area and reveals finer flaws. The test applies to any non-porous material, magnetic or not.

The method only reveals flaws that are open to the surface. A crack closed by grinding, peening, blasting or smeared metal may show nothing, and a flaw filled with oil, paint, polymer or corrosion product will not accept penetrant. Rough castings, porous materials and uneven weld surfaces produce confusing backgrounds. PT tells you nothing about depth or about flaws below the surface, so when wall thickness or a buried weld defect is the question, use ultrasonic testing in Lake Charles. For carbon steel crack detection, magnetic particle testing in Lake Charles is often faster.

Codes and material controls

The method is controlled by ASME Section V Article 6, with ASTM E165 as the practice for general industry and ASTM E1417 as a related standard. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 gives PT methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, and ASME B31.3 section 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 covers process piping. The owner's inspection program decides which applies to in-service repairs, and the authorized inspector is responsible for the conclusion. We supply the examination record.

Material cleanliness is a particular concern on corrosion-resistant alloys. When penetrant materials are used on austenitic stainless steel or nickel-base alloys, the sulfur and halogen content of the products must be controlled, because residues can trigger cracking or pitting during later heating or service. We record the lot and the certification of the cleaner, penetrant, remover and developer on the report. Louisiana's boiler rules, administered through the Office of State Fire Marshal's Boiler Inspection Section, rely on commissioned inspectors for units that fall under them, and our report goes to that person for repairs to such equipment. Read our explanation of the Article 6 requirements for details.

How the examination proceeds

Preparation takes most of the effort. The technician removes slag, scale, paint and oil from the weld and the adjacent base metal, cleans with an approved solvent or detergent, and allows the surface to dry completely. If a surface has been blasted, peened or machined so that flaws may be smeared closed, the procedure may require light etching to open them. Poor cleaning is the main reason penetrant tests fail to find real cracks.

Penetrant goes on by spray, brush or dip and stays for a specified dwell time that depends on the material, the likely flaws and the temperature. Excess is removed with solvent-dampened wipes for solvent-removable systems or a controlled water rinse for water-washable ones, taking care not to over-wash. A thin, even coat of developer is applied, and the surface is read during and after the development time. Indications are evaluated by shape, size and location and compared with the acceptance criteria. Comparator blocks and system checks confirm the materials are working before a job starts.

Heat, humidity and hurricane season

Louisiana summers put real pressure on penetrant work. ASME Section V sets a standard window of roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials; outside it the procedure has to be demonstrated for the actual temperature. Stainless pipe on a rack in the afternoon sun can run well past the upper limit, and solvent penetrant then flashes off before it can enter a flaw. In practice that means early-morning starts, shade, or a high-temperature procedure. High humidity slows drying of cleaners and developer, and sudden showers wash out penetrant or ruin a developer coat.

Hurricane season and its aftermath matter too. After the 2020 storms, plants spent long periods in repair and restart, and weld repairs on stainless and alloy equipment kept PT busy long after the weather cleared. We keep plans flexible for storm shutdowns and recommend that owners put weather holds in the schedule.

Cryogenic and LNG piping

LNG facilities add a specific PT workload. Liquefaction and storage systems use stainless steel and aluminum piping suited to very low temperatures, and the welds on those systems are usually examined by penetrant. Surface cracks in a cryogenic weld can grow under thermal cycling, so owners ask for a documented surface check after fabrication and after repairs. The same applies to cold-box and exchanger welds in gas processing. Cleanliness is a concern because penetrant residue on a cryogenic line is unwelcome, so cleaning and final removal steps get as much attention as the test itself, and the owner often specifies approved materials.

Heat exchangers, overlays and clad surfaces

Chemical and refining units have many shell-and-tube exchangers. The welds that join tubes to the tubesheet are small and numerous, and a surface crack at one of them can send process fluid into the cooling side. After retubing or repair, a penetrant check of the tube-to-tubesheet welds, where the design allows access, gives a reliable record. Reactors, columns and drums with weld overlay or clad linings are also examined for surface cracks at nozzle welds and repair areas. Because the lining alloy is usually stainless or nickel-base, penetrant is the natural method.

Owners who buy penetrant work for the first time often ask how much of the surface to cover. The procedure answers that: the weld plus a margin of base metal on each side, set by the code or the engineer. For tube-to-tubesheet welds it is each weld, for overlays it is the area named in the repair plan. We confirm the extent in writing before starting, so the report and the scope agree.

Another practical point is waste and cleanup. Used wipes, cleaners and developer are collected and handled under the plant's rules, and technicians leave the area clean, which matters in chemical units where residue could affect the process or the next inspector's work.

Documenting repairs after storm and outage work

Large outages and storm recovery generate hundreds of weld repairs. The usual pattern is to excavate a defect, check the cavity by penetrant or magnetic particle depending on the material, weld the repair, grind it flush and examine it again. Each stage is recorded against the weld number so that the owner's inspector can see the sequence. We keep a clean log of weld numbers, dates, materials and results, with photographs of the prepared surfaces and the final indication map, so the repair file is ready for the owner's quality records without rework.

Where repair welds are made on equipment that comes under Louisiana's boiler and pressure vessel rules, the commissioned inspector needs the same examination record, and the report is laid out to make that easy.

Who does the work and who reviews it

PT is performed by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which is based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II prepares the surface, runs the test and evaluates indications; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and checks the reporting. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer issues certification, so each technician's qualification is defined by the written practice of the company that employs them. If you need a project procedure or an independent review of penetrant work, see Level III consulting and written practice development.

What the report contains

The report names the part or weld by tag, drawing or weld number, with the procedure revision, code edition and acceptance criteria. It lists the penetrant system and method, cleaner, remover and developer with lot numbers, surface temperature, dwell and development times, and the lighting for fluorescent work. Each indication is described by location, shape and size and marked relevant or non-relevant and accepted or rejected. Photographs, sketches and notes on final cleaning give the reviewer the full sequence.

Choosing among PT, MT and UT in Lake Charles

Penetrant is the practical choice for non-magnetic alloys, small or irregular parts, and checks of repaired surfaces. Magnetic particle is usually better for crack detection in carbon steel structure. Ultrasonics is the answer for wall loss and buried flaws. See the MT versus PT comparison, the national penetrant testing page, and the Louisiana inspection page for broader planning. Atlantis has no office in Lake Charles, technicians mobilize to your site, and we reply within one business day to a quote request.

Training in-house penetrant technicians

Companies in the Lake Charles area can train their own people with PT Level 1 and PT Level 2, use the penetrant testing simulator and see the Lake Charles training page.

faq.q: Why is penetrant testing used so often on Lake Charles chemical equipment?
faq.a: Many chemical and LNG components are stainless, duplex, nickel alloy or aluminum, which cannot be magnetized. Penetrant testing finds surface-breaking cracks in those welds and also works on carbon steel when magnetic particle is awkward.

faq.q: Can PT find cracks that do not reach the surface?
faq.a: No. Only flaws open to the surface take up penetrant. Subsurface cracks, lack of fusion inside a weld and wall loss call for ultrasonic testing instead.

faq.q: Does hot weather affect dye penetrant inspection?
faq.a: Yes. The standard window under ASME Section V is about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Louisiana summer surfaces can exceed it, so work moves to early hours, shade, or a procedure qualified for the higher temperature.

faq.q: Do you control halogens and sulfur for work on stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes. When the code or owner requires it, we use penetrant materials with controlled sulfur and halogen content and record the lot certification in the report to show it was verified.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Lake Charles office?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Lake Charles. We mobilize technicians to your site for the agreed scope and plan travel, orientation and permits during the quoting stage.

faq.q: What surface preparation do you need before PT?
faq.a: The test area should be free of loose scale, paint, oil and spatter and dry. Our technician finishes the cleaning, and the procedure states when grinding or etching is also needed to open possible flaws.

faq.q: Is fluorescent penetrant better than visible dye?
faq.a: Fluorescent systems reveal finer cracks, though they demand a dim work area and an ultraviolet lamp. Visible red dye is read in ordinary light, which suits quick field checks. Your procedure names which type may be used.

faq.q: Who reviews the PT results?
faq.a: A Level II technician performs and interprets the test, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and report format. The owner’s inspector or engineer makes the final acceptance decision for the equipment.

faq.q: Can your team train our Lake Charles staff in penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Our PT Level 1 and Level 2 courses follow SNT-TC-1A. Your company then qualifies and certifies its technicians under its own written practice after the experience hours are completed.
